answers.answer:
Short version: you started with a game, then cut the game and kept the agent.

The original pitch was productivity as an idle game — Cookie Clicker, except the little workers are real AI agents doing your actual tasks in the background, and you spend the time you'd have spent doomscrolling directing them instead. You even added the room layer: you'd customize the agents' rooms and watch them work, addictive in a good way.

Then you changed your mind. The game layer was a distraction, and you said the honest reason out loud: you'd spend all your time on the art. So the rooms and customization got cut, and what was left was the core — proactive agents that keep a model of your life and reach out with what you could do right now.

What actually survived the cut is the part that has to work rather than the part that's fun: self-explaining storage is what lets an agent show why it's suggesting something right now, and the OS analogy is your attempt at specifying how those agents juggle tasks without letting one task's state leak into another.

The thing I'd flag: cutting the game layer also cut the low-stakes interface. What protected the original idea from becoming a second job was that you could ignore it for a day and come back to something legible. With that gone, the checkable reason on each nudge is doing all the protection work now — so that's the piece to keep an eye on.

You started with productivity as an idle game: real AI agents doing your actual tasks in the background while you direct them instead of doomscrolling, with customizable rooms you'd watch them work in — addictive in a good way.

Then you cut it. The game layer was the distraction, you said you'd spend all your time on the art, and the real core was proactive agents that hold a model of your life and reach out with what you could do right now. So the rooms and customization went, which was the part I'd flagged as both the pull and the risky bit.

What survived got more concrete. You framed a multi-task agent as an operating system — each paused task keeping sealed state, a finished job acting like an interrupt that loads one task, runs it, switches back, nothing leaking. Then agents that dream: idle time spent going over everything at full depth to form new connections, not to answer anything. That became a desk agent paging books in from a self-explaining library, parked tasks, and an overnight pass reorganizing in the background.

So the arc: from a game you'd play, to a system that works while you sleep.

answers.answer:
Three clearly. The OS one is the explicit borrow: paused tasks keeping saved state, background jobs arriving as interrupts, context swapped without leaking — that's literally how operating systems switch processes[k59]. The dreaming idea is the brain borrow: idle time going over everything at full depth to form new connections is sleep consolidation, and you named it that way yourself[k42].

The desk-versus-library one is a computer borrow too, less obviously — the desk is a cache or a context window, small and fast, backed by a big slow store you page in on demand[k1]. And the idle game is a softer one: it's not borrowing a mechanism from either, it's borrowing the shape of an existing genre and asking what happens if the little workers are real[k11].

The one I'd flag as not really a borrow: the desk/library thing started as a picture of how remembering should feel and only later got matched onto registers and disk. That's you reaching for the metaphor, not the machine handing you one.

Worth separating two kinds of borrow, since you asked which: dreaming and the OS are mechanism borrows — you're saying the system should work the way the real thing does. Desk/library and the idle game are interface borrows — they give you a picture to think with, but neither claims the underlying machinery is the same. The mechanism ones are where you have to earn the analogy; the interface ones are allowed to be loose.

And the seam to watch: the OS borrow promises a cheap automatic switch, but a finished agent task is a judgment call, not a hardware signal, so that's where the machine metaphor stops paying[k61].

answers.answer:
The pitch should hang on your own metaphor, since it's the clearest thing you've said about the project: the context window is a desk — small, and whatever's on it is all the agent can see — and the fix is to make the agent a researcher in a library instead, where it doesn't need to know everything up front because the structure lets it find things, read one book, and follow its footnotes to the next[k1][k3]. From there, two threads make it a system rather than a metaphor. First, the reason requirement: whatever the agent stored, suggested, or paged in has to carry its own checkable reason, because that's what makes the structure navigable cold and what lets an unprompted nudge land as help instead of noise[k18]. Second, the two halves that run while you're not asking for anything — proactive agents holding a model of your life and reaching out, and the idle dream pass that reorganizes and makes new edges in the background without reaching out itself[k25][k42][k45]. And you've already got a test and a first live case to close on: the fork test, where you stop a conversation, continue it once from the transcript and once from memory alone, and have a blind judge compare — that's the check on whether the model actually stands in for the conversation[k73] — and the radiator week as the first concrete time-triggered nudge it has to get right[k55]. If the paragraph needs one sentence of "why now," it's that the prototype is small enough to run on that.

One caution on the frame: the fork test is only weak evidence of preservation and strong evidence of loss, since a judge is reading the desk, and part of what carries a self never shows up in a single reply. Don't overclaim it in the pitch.
